product-sum-rule.name: Product and sum rules
product-sum-rule.summary: Multiply for steps that all happen; add for either/or choices.
how: If a choice happens in steps, and step one has $a$ options and step two has $b$ options whatever you picked first, there are $a \times b$ ways to do both.
If you pick exactly one option from group A *or* group B, and no option is in both, there are $a + b$ ways.

formulas.when: step 1 has a options, then step 2 has b options
one choice from A or from B, with no overlap

product-sum-rule.example: An outfit is a shirt (4 kinds) and trousers (3 kinds), so $4 \times 3 = 12$ outfits. A snack that is fruit (4 kinds) or a biscuit (3 kinds) gives $4 + 3 = 7$ snacks.
product-sum-rule.trap: Adding when both steps happen (or multiplying when only one happens). Ask "do I make both choices, or one of them?"

permutations.name: Permutations
permutations.summary: Arrange items in order; every item is different.
how: Fill the positions one at a time. The first position has $n$ choices, the next $n-1$ (one item is used up), and so on.
Lining up all $n$ items gives $n!$. Filling only $k$ positions gives $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$, written $P(n,k)$.

formulas.when: arrange all n different items in a row
arrange k of the n items (order matters)

permutations.example: Gold, silver and bronze among 8 runners is $P(8,3) = 8 \times 7 \times 6 = 336$.
permutations.trap: Using $P(n,k)$ when order doesn't matter. A team of 3 is not a podium of 3.

combinations.name: Combinations
combinations.summary: Choose a group; order doesn't matter.
how: Count ordered picks with $P(n,k)$, then notice each group of $k$ was counted once for every order of its members, $k!$ times.
Divide that out: $C(n,k) = \frac{P(n,k)}{k!}$.

formulas.when: choose k of n different items, order doesn't matter
why it works, ordered picks divided by the orders of each group

combinations.trap: Multiplying several $C$'s for groups that are really the same kind of choice (choosing 3 people as "1, then 2 more" counts each committee several times).

multiset-permutations.name: Repeated items
multiset-permutations.summary: Arrange items where some are identical.
how: Pretend every item is different and arrange them: $n!$ ways.
Identical items swapping places give the same arrangement, so divide by the orders of each group of repeats.

formulas.when: a items of one kind and b of another
three kinds of repeated items

multiset-permutations.example: The letters of BANANA (one B, two N's, three A's) make $\frac{6!}{1!\,2!\,3!} = 60$ different words.
multiset-permutations.trap: Dividing by $n!$ for every letter, or forgetting a group that repeats.

stars-and-bars.name: Stars and bars
stars-and-bars.summary: Share identical items among distinct groups.
how: Line the items up as stars and drop in bars to cut the line into groups. With $k$ groups you need $k-1$ bars.
Every arrangement of the stars and bars is exactly one way to share the items, so count the ways to choose which of the $n+k-1$ spots hold bars.

formulas.when: n identical items, k groups, a group may get nothing
every group gets at least one
the minimums add up to m, so hand those out first

stars-and-bars.example: 7 identical cookies for 3 kids is $C(9,2) = 36$ ways. ★★★ | | ★★★★ means A gets 3, B gets 0, C gets 4.
stars-and-bars.trap: The items must be identical. 7 different cookies for 3 kids is $3^7$ (each cookie picks a kid), not stars and bars.

inclusion-exclusion.name: Inclusion–exclusion
inclusion-exclusion.summary: Count a union by adding the groups and subtracting the overlaps.
how: Adding $|A| + |B|$ counts everything in both groups twice, so subtract the overlap once.
With three groups, the pairwise overlaps get subtracted too often, so add back the part in all three. The signs alternate with the size of the overlap.

formulas.when: the groups have a and b items, and x items are in both

formulas.latex: a + b + c - x - y - z + t
formulas.when: x, y, z are the pairwise overlaps and t is in all three

inclusion-exclusion.example: Of 30 students, 18 play football, 12 play chess and 5 do both, so $18 + 12 - 5 = 25$ do at least one.
inclusion-exclusion.trap: Stopping after the pairs with three groups; the triple overlap must be added back.

derangements.name: Derangements
derangements.summary: Count arrangements where nothing lands in its own place.
how: Start with all $n!$ arrangements and remove the bad ones, where someone gets their own item.

Fix $k$ chosen people in their own places, $C(n,k)$ ways, and shuffle the rest freely, $(n-k)!$ ways. Overlaps get counted several times, so alternate the signs: subtract $k = 1$, add back $k = 2$, and so on.
Simplifying $C(n,k)(n-k)! = \frac{n!}{k!}$ gives the short form.

formulas.when: the alternating sum, straight from the reasoning
the same number, simplified

derangements.example: For 3 hats, $3! - 3 \cdot 2! + 3 \cdot 1! - 1 = 6 - 6 + 3 - 1 = 2$, namely BCA and CAB.
derangements.trap: Subtracting $C(n,1)(n-1)!$ only. Arrangements where two people match were removed twice and must be added back.

complement.name: Complement
complement.summary: Count everything, then subtract what you don't want.
how: Problems that say "at least one" split into many cases. The opposite, "none", is usually one simple count.
Count the total, count the opposite, and subtract.

formulas.when: t outcomes in total, b of them are the ones you don't want
n dice rolls (in order) with at least one 6

complement.example: 4 dice rolls with at least one 6 give $6^4 - 5^4 = 1296 - 625 = 671$ lists.
complement.trap: Using "exactly one" as the opposite of "at least one". The opposite is "none".

symmetry-relative-order.name: Symmetry
symmetry-relative-order.summary: When every order of some items is equally common, take your share.
how: Look only at where a few chosen items sit relative to each other. Across all arrangements, each of their $r!$ relative orders turns up equally often.
So the arrangements where they appear in one particular order are $\frac{1}{r!}$ of all of them.

formulas.when: r chosen items must appear in one given order among n
A comes somewhere before B

symmetry-relative-order.example: 5 people in a line with Ann somewhere before Ben: half of $5! = 120$, so 60.
symmetry-relative-order.trap: Fixing positions you weren't asked to fix. "Before" means anywhere earlier, not right next to.

choose-then-order.name: Choose, then order
choose-then-order.summary: Pick who is involved, then arrange or assign roles.
how: Split the job into "which items?" and "in what arrangement?".
Choose the group with $C(n,k)$, then multiply by the ways to arrange it, $k!$ for a row, or the number of role choices.

formulas.when: choose k of n, then line them up
choose a team of k, then one of them as captain

choose-then-order.example: A 4-person team with a captain from 9 people: $C(9,4) \times 4 = 504$.
choose-then-order.trap: Ordering the team and also naming a captain, which counts each team in several orders.

glue-block.name: Glue into a block
glue-block.summary: Items that must stay together move as one block.
how: Glue the items that must be together into one block and arrange the block with the other items.
Then arrange the items inside the block.

formulas.when: k of the n items must be next to each other in a row

glue-block.example: 6 friends in a row with 2 who insist on sitting together: $5! \times 2! = 240$.
glue-block.trap: Forgetting the $k!$ orders inside the block.

gap-method.name: Gap method
gap-method.summary: Keep items apart by placing the others first, then using the gaps.
how: Arrange the unrestricted items first. They leave gaps between them and at both ends, one more gap than items.
Put each item that must stay apart into a different gap.

formulas.when: n different items in a row, k of them may not be next to each other
choose k of n places in a row with no two next to each other

gap-method.example: 3 girls and 4 boys in a row with no two girls together: $4! \times P(5,3) = 1440$.
gap-method.trap: Counting only the gaps between items and forgetting the two ends.

restricted-first.name: Restricted first
restricted-first.summary: Place the fussy items first, then fill in the rest.
how: Items with conditions have fewer options, so deal with them before anything else.
Once they're placed, the remaining items go anywhere.

formulas.when: one person in a row of n must not stand at either end

restricted-first.example: 5 people in a row, Ann not at either end: Ann has 3 spots, the rest $4!$, so $72$.
restricted-first.trap: Placing free items first, which makes the fussy item's options depend on earlier choices.

divide-overcounting.name: Divide out overcounting
divide-overcounting.summary: Count with labels, then divide by the orders that don't matter.
how: Count as if everything were labelled or ordered; that is often easy.
Each real outcome was counted once for every relabelling that changes nothing, so divide by that number.

formulas.when: split 2m people into m pairs, where pairs have no names
split a·g people into g unnamed groups of a

divide-overcounting.trap: Dividing by $g!$ when the groups do have names (Team Red and Team Blue).

circular.name: Circular arrangements
circular.summary: Around a table, rotations are the same seating.
how: A row of $n$ people has $n!$ orders, but turning the table gives the same seating, and each seating appears $n$ times.
So there are $\frac{n!}{n} = (n-1)!$ seatings. Equivalently, seat one person first to fix the turning, then arrange the rest.
If flipping over also counts as the same (bracelets), halve again.

formulas.when: n people around a round table
n different beads on a bracelet (rotations and flips), n at least 3

circular.example: 5 people at a round table: $4! = 24$ seatings.
circular.trap: Halving for a table. People at a table see left and right differently, so flips are not the same seating.

lattice-paths.name: Lattice paths
lattice-paths.summary: Paths on a grid are choices of which steps go right.
how: A path from the corner to $a$ right and $b$ up is a list of $a$ R's and $b$ U's in some order.
Choose which of the $a+b$ steps are R's.
To pass through a point, count the paths to it and from it, then multiply.

formulas.when: a steps right and b steps up
paths that pass through the point (c, d)

lattice-paths.example: To go 4 right and 3 up: $C(7,4) = 35$ paths.
lattice-paths.trap: Using $2^{a+b}$, which allows paths that overshoot the corner.

balls-into-boxes.name: Balls into boxes
balls-into-boxes.summary: Ask whether the balls and the boxes are different.
how: Different balls into different boxes means each ball picks its box on its own.
To keep every box non-empty, subtract the ways that leave boxes empty, with inclusion–exclusion.
Identical balls into different boxes is stars and bars.

formulas.when: n different balls into k different boxes
every box gets at least one ball
n identical balls into k different boxes

balls-into-boxes.trap: Using $n^k$. Each ball makes the choice, so the number of boxes is the base.

pigeonhole.name: Pigeonhole
pigeonhole.summary: More items than boxes forces two to share.
how: Put items into boxes as evenly as you can. With $k$ boxes, $k$ items can all go in different boxes, but item $k + 1$ must join one of them.
To force a box with $r$ items, fill every box with $r - 1$ first; one more forces it.

formulas.when: fewest items that force two in the same box
fewest items that force r in the same box

pigeonhole.example: There are 12 months, so among any 13 people two share a birth month.
pigeonhole.trap: Answering $k$. With exactly $k$ items everyone can still be in a different box.

binomial-identities.name: Binomial identities
binomial-identities.summary: Count one thing in two ways, and the two answers are equal.
how: Pick a question, like "how many groups can you choose?", and answer it in two different ways. Both answers count the same thing, so they're equal.
Pascal's rule splits groups by whether they include one special person.

formulas.when: groups with the special person, plus groups without
all groups of every size, or each person in or out
choose k from a boys and b girls, split by how many boys

binomial-identities.trap: Checking an identity on one number instead of explaining why both sides count the same thing.
